free.name: Pixellot
free.hq: Israel, with US offices in Atlanta and Durham
free.payer_model_label: Platform pays for cameras and shares revenue
free.one_line: Pixellot builds fixed multi-sensor cameras (Show S3) and a portable one (Air NXT) that produce and stream matches unattended, and sells the output through platform partners such as PlayOn in US high schools and through a direct Pixellot You shop for clubs [pix-04, pix-02, pix-06].
free.who_for: Federations, leagues, school networks and streaming platforms that want hundreds of venues producing live games with graphics and ads and a revenue share on the audience, plus clubs that buy an Air NXT and a Team or Club plan for their own coaching video [pix-01, pix-05]. Football clubs in Italy get the Air NXT at 999 euros with plans from 1,009 euros per year, and professional academies such as Fiorentina have used the fixed system across a whole training centre [pix-05, pix-10].
free.why: Pixellot exists because live production of youth sport only pays when a camera costs less than one camera operator per season, and its fixed systems in 9,000 US schools proved that model at scale [pix-01]. It matters now because the November 2025 PlayOn extension and the January 2026 35 million dollar raise moved the company from selling cameras to sharing revenue on the content the cameras generate, which it calls AI as a Service [pix-02, pix-01]. That tells you where the space is going, with capture becoming a cost line inside a media business and the vendor's income tied to viewership and monetisation, with hardware reduced to an enabler [pix-21].
free.price_band: Pixellot You direct shop: Air NXT €999 plus €1,009 (Team) or €1,299 (Club) per year in the EU price list; fixed Show systems and partner deployments are quote-only or revenue-share

italy.note: Fiorentina chose Pixellot for nine pitches at its new training centre in June 2022 and the Lega Nazionale Dilettanti streamed all 114 group matches of the 2023 Torneo delle Regioni with Pixellot technology, while the Pixellot You shop routes Italian demo requests to a local reseller calendar and offers an Italian-language storefront [pix-10, pix-11, pix-05].

free.evidence_note: Direct-to-club prices come from the price tables embedded in the Pixellot You site script for EU, US and UK markets, and corporate claims from Pixellot press releases; the company is private with no published accounts, fixed-system pricing is quote-only, and reviewer volume is small, so several judgements rest on vendor statements and trade press.

free.name: Sportway (incl. MyGame)
free.payer_model_label: Platform pays for cameras and shares revenue
free.one_line: Sportway installs fixed AI cameras in arenas and on pitches at its own cost, produces every match automatically and distributes it through federation branded OTT platforms and consumer services such as MyGame in Norway [sportway-03, sportway-04, sportway-11].
free.who_for: Federations, leagues and media groups that want a whole tier of sport filmed and monetised without asking clubs to buy anything, plus the clubs inside those deals that receive cameras, coaching tools and a revenue share for free [sportway-06, sportway-11, sportway-12]. Individual clubs outside a federation agreement have no public way to buy in.
free.why: Sportway exists because Nordic ice hockey and handball federations wanted every game on a screen and no club would pay for a camera, so the company took on the capital cost and built a rights and subscription business around it, reaching about 2,500 cameras in 21 countries and 250,000 events a year by June 2026 [sportway-01]. It matters now because the June 2026 EUR 20 million round led by Giorgio Chiellini's Gamma Waves, the Studio Automated acquisition and the KNHB ClubhockeyTV deal show the model exporting beyond Scandinavia and into football adjacent sports [sportway-01, sportway-11, sportway-15]. It tells you the grassroots video market is splitting into a consumer camera business and a rights infrastructure business, and Sportway is the clearest European example of the second, with the Norwegian consent fights around MyGame as the cautionary tale [sportway-08, sportway-09].
free.price_band: Clubs pay nothing for cameras or installation under federation deals; consumers pay NOK 139/month or NOK 1,199/year for MyGame in Norway with 20% returned to a chosen club; Playsite and federation platform fees are not public

italy.note: Sportway has a Milan operating base and a partnership with the Italian Ice Sports Federation (FISG) since autumn 2023 covering about 35 ice venues in ice hockey, figure skating, speed skating and curling, with a stated aim to expand beyond ice sports [sportway-02].

free.evidence_note: Consumer pricing, federation deals, funding and company registry data come from primary sources; camera hardware specifications, club level commercial terms and consolidated financials are not public, and privacy history relies on Norwegian press.

free.name: Staige (Staige One AG, formerly soccerwatch.tv)
free.payer_model_label: Platform pays for cameras and shares revenue
free.one_line: A fixed 180-degree AI camera bolted to a floodlight pole that streams amateur matches to the Staige TV platform, sells virtual tickets and sponsor banners on the club's behalf, and feeds a coaching app.
free.who_for: German-speaking amateur and semi-professional clubs that want every home match streamed without a volunteer behind a camera, and that have a sponsor or a regional bank willing to fund the hardware. Federations and broadcasters that want a turnkey lower-league feed are the second audience.
free.why: Staige exists because soccerwatch.tv proved in 2017 that German amateur clubs would let a robot camera film them if the stream came with sponsor money attached, and the K2 panorama camera plus the Staige TV paywall turned that into a repeatable product with more than 250,000 events recorded [staige-06]. It matters now because the listed parent Staige One AG has spent 2025 and 2026 moving its capital and its engineers into Staige for Industries, a security and infrastructure video business, while the sport segment sits flat at about €2.0 million revenue and camera deliveries run behind schedule [staige-05, staige-07]. It tells you that the pure sponsor-funded amateur streaming model, on its own, has struggled to carry a listed company, and that the survivors in this space will be the ones with a second revenue engine or a very lean cost base.
free.price_band: Camera pricing on request, typically sponsor or bank funded; €1.50 net per paid pay-per-view access retained by Staige

italy.note: The 2025 annual report lists Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, the USA and China as markets and does not mention Italy, and an earlier regional profile named Italy only as an expansion target [staige-05, staige-10].

free.evidence_note: Company health, shareholders, headcount and the €1.50 pay-per-view fee are verified from the audited annual report, stock exchange releases and the vendor site; camera purchase and subscription prices are not published anywhere public, and installed camera counts come from the vendor.
free.flag: Going-concern note in the FY2025 accounts

free.name: BEPRO (Bepro Company Co., Ltd. / Bepro Europe GmbH)
free.hq: Seoul, South Korea, with European entity in Hamburg and group entities in London
free.payer_model_label: Club pays for a coaching tool
free.one_line: A Korean-founded analysis company that sells a fixed or portable dual-lens 4K panoramic camera bundled with a cloud analysis suite, human-verified event data and optional video-based tracking data, aimed at academies and semi-professional clubs.
free.who_for: Academies, semi-professional first teams and federations that already employ an analyst and want FIFA-qualified panoramic footage plus tagged event data delivered back within a day, with the option to add tracking-derived physical metrics without GPS vests. Fan streaming is a side benefit.
free.why: BEPRO exists because a Seoul team of analysts worked out in 2015 that the expensive part of football data was the human tagging, and that if you controlled the camera you could industrialise the tagging and sell it to clubs the big data houses ignored [bepro-12, bepro-20]. It matters now because the 2025 Cerberus OS3 release with RTMP live coding into Sportscode, the Camera Station that accepts any IP camera, and published dollar pricing for the portable kit mark a shift from bespoke fixed installs toward a self-serve product for smaller clubs [bepro-10, bepro-09, bepro-02]. It tells you that the analysis-first vendors are moving down market into the same academies that Veo and Pixellot serve from the streaming side, and that data delivered with the video, ahead of the camera itself, is where they intend to win.
free.price_band: USD 2,000 one-off for the Cerberus portable camera plus USD 1,000 per year (or USD 83.33 per month) for BEPRO Space and Editor software, VAT excluded; fixed camera and event data services on quotation

italy.note: BEPRO lists Italy among its office countries, has been the video analysis partner of the Divisione Calcio a 5 for Serie A futsal with a renewal announced in October 2024, and installed fixed cameras at Bologna FC's youth training grounds in December 2020 under an Italian business director [bepro-08, bepro-15, bepro-16].

free.evidence_note: Portable camera, software, quadpod and platform prices are read directly from the vendor's pages in USD; fixed camera and data service prices are on quotation; corporate financials for the Korean parent are not public and the Hamburg entity's latest filed accounts are for 2021.

free.name: Hudl Focus
free.payer_model_label: Club pays for a coaching tool
free.one_line: Hudl Focus is the camera family of the Hudl analysis platform, with fixed Indoor and Outdoor units, a static Focus Point and the portable Focus Flex, all of which upload automatically into a Hudl subscription that is required to use them [hf-01, hf-07].
free.who_for: Clubs and academies that already live inside Hudl, Sportscode or Wyscout and want the film to arrive without an operator, with the Flex packaged for semi-professional and amateur football from 2,000 dollars including a Bronze subscription [hf-03, hf-11]. US schools that want a permanent stadium or gym camera with livestreaming to Hudl TV, since broadcasting is limited to the fixed units [hf-01, hf-07].
free.why: Hudl Focus exists because Hudl owned the coaching workflow and needed to own the capture point too, so the camera is sold as a way to feed the subscription, and it has never been priced as a product in its own right [hf-07, hf-05]. It matters now because the Flex, refreshed in February 2024 with a three-hour battery and automatic calibration, is the only portable camera bundled with Assist stat breakdowns and Wyscout tagging, which makes Hudl the incumbent choice for any club that already pays for those tools [hf-09, hf-12, hf-03]. It tells you the space is consolidating around platforms, with Hudl adding Balltime, Titan and TeamUp in 2025 and 2026 while publishing no camera price and no Focus product news at all [hf-17, hf-18].
free.price_band: Focus cameras carry no list price and are sold inside quoted club or athletic-department packages; the one published camera bundle is the mid-market soccer Team Pack from USD 2,000 with a Flex; soccer software runs USD 500 to 2,500 per team per year (Core, Plus, Premier), US high school programs USD 1,500 to 4,000 per program per year, and every sport and segment has its own price grid [hf-03, hf-23, hf-24, hf-25]

italy.note: Hudl owns Wyscout, headquartered in Chiavari, and publishes Italian-language Focus Flex content aimed at amateur football, but no Italian club deployment of Focus is documented and 4G streaming on the Flex is US-only [hf-20, hf-12, hf-06].

free.evidence_note: Package and subscription prices come from Hudl pricing pages, product facts from Hudl pages, FAQs and blog posts, and security and privacy from Hudl policies; camera unit prices, specifications such as resolution and warranty terms are unpublished, and the company is private with no financial disclosure.

free.name: Once Sport (Once Sport d.o.o.)
free.payer_model_label: Club pays for a coaching tool
free.one_line: Desktop software from a Zagreb video analysis company that turns wide-angle footage from a Reolink camera, two GoPros or any panoramic source into an auto-followed broadcast-style video, with live streaming to YouTube and an optional €5 per match cloud processing service.
free.who_for: Coaches, analysts and small clubs that already own or can buy a cheap wide-angle camera and a reasonable PC, and who want automated match video for a few tens of euros a month, with no proprietary camera or locked cloud. Football academies in Portugal, Spain, Croatia, the UK and Italy make up the visible user base.
free.why: Once Sport exists because a video analysis software house realised that the expensive part of a Veo or Pixellot is the proprietary camera and cloud, and that a good tracking model running on the coach's own laptop could deliver the same virtual camera from commodity hardware [once-sport-01, once-sport-07]. It matters now because at €19 or €38 a month with hardware you source yourself, and €5 a match in the cloud, it undercuts every integrated system by an order of magnitude at the moment budgets at amateur clubs are being squeezed [once-sport-03]. It tells you that automated match video is being unbundled into camera, processing and platform, and that the processing layer is on its way to becoming a cheap software subscription.
free.price_band: €19/month Autocam Personal or €38/month Autocam Club, tax excluded, yearly billing at nine times the monthly rate; €5 per match cloud processing; camera hardware bought separately

italy.note: AS Lodigiani Calcio 1972 in Rome uses Autocam, Analyser and Coach Board across its academy and first team per a March 2025 case study, the software ships with an Italian interface and pricing table, and the company exhibited at The Coach Experience in Rimini in June 2025 [once-sport-08, once-sport-03, once-sport-06].

free.evidence_note: All subscription and per-match prices are read directly from the vendor's live pricing table data in EUR and USD, product behaviour comes from vendor pages and dated release posts, and the corporate record is confirmed from the Croatian company registry; hardware prices for the recommended cameras are not published by the vendor.

free.name: Provispo B.V.
free.payer_model_label: Club pays for a coaching tool
free.one_line: A small Dutch integrator that installs fixed dual-camera panoramic and PTZ systems at professional training grounds, runs them from its PlayStats cloud, and has added a portable on-device 180-degree camera called SportCam Go for lower budgets.
free.who_for: Professional academies and federation training centres in the Benelux and Portugal that want owned camera infrastructure across several pitches, open export to Hudl, Sportscode or Nacsport, and RTSP feeds for live analysis. The SportCam Go targets amateur clubs and single-team analysts who want the same openness without the install.
free.why: Provispo exists because Dutch and Belgian academies wanted cameras that behaved like infrastructure they owned, with scheduled recording, local storage and plain MP4 downloads, with no closed subscription platform in the way, and a one-person Terneuzen company built that for Feyenoord, AZ, Genk and Royal Antwerp [provispo-01, provispo-03, provispo-09]. It matters now because the SportCam Go, with onboard processing, RTSP access and a 10-hour battery, takes that analyst-first, open-export philosophy into the portable segment where Veo and Pixellot sell closed clouds [provispo-02, provispo-08]. It tells you that the fight in this space is shifting from who has the best AI camera operator to who lets the club keep control of the footage and the workflow.
free.price_band: No prices published; all systems including SportCam Go are quoted after consultation

italy.note: No Italian client, reseller or office appears on the vendor site, in its news or in the company record, and the stated federation work covers the Netherlands, Belgium and Portugal [provispo-01, provispo-03].

free.evidence_note: Product features and client names come from the vendor site only, no price is public anywhere, the federation relationships could not be confirmed from the federations' side, and the only registry data shows a one-employee company with no filed financial detail.

free.name: Reeplayer
free.payer_model_label: Club pays for a coaching tool
free.one_line: Reeplayer sells a US made three lens soccer camera with on device AI and a built in SIM for USD 1,499 plus USD 99 a month, streams every game live for free, and since July 2026 offers to give teams the camera when a local brand sponsors it [reeplayer-01, reeplayer-05].
free.who_for: American youth and amateur soccer teams that want instant livestreams and quick uploads without a parent managing hotspots or ethernet cables, and club directors willing to try an advertising funded camera [reeplayer-01, reeplayer-06]. The company states it is available only in the United States and only for soccer [reeplayer-01, reeplayer-03].
free.why: Reeplayer exists because a Los Angeles founding team decided the cure for slow uploads and dead hotspots was a camera with its own cellular modem and an NVIDIA Jetson doing the AI on the sideline, and it raised USD 10 million in 2023 to build that in Pittsburgh [reeplayer-08, reeplayer-10]. It matters now because the July 2026 End Pay-to-Play initiative tries to move the bill from families to brands, with 40% of advertising profit returned to the team, which is the first serious attempt in this market to turn the camera from a cost into a media asset [reeplayer-05, reeplayer-06]. It tells you that whoever controls the livestream of youth games controls an audience, and that vendors are starting to price accordingly.
free.price_band: USD 1,499 camera + USD 349 tripod one off, plus USD 1,188/yr (USD 99/month billed annually) or USD 2,700 per three years; sponsor funded option at USD 0 to the team where a brand signs

italy.note: Reeplayer states the product is exclusively available in the United States and the built in data plan is tied to US carriers, so there is no Italian or European availability [reeplayer-01, reeplayer-03].

free.evidence_note: Pricing, features and availability are verified from Reeplayer's own pages; hardware architecture comes from the manufacturing partner Hellbender; funding and the sponsorship model come from trade press and Crunchbase; camera resolution and independent reliability data are not published.

free.name: Spiideo
free.payer_model_label: Club pays for a coaching tool
free.one_line: Spiideo installs cloud-connected fixed cameras (S-Line, X-Line, D-Line, A-Line) on pitches and arenas and sells a cloud suite on top, led by Spiideo Perform for coaches and analysts and Spiideo Play for automated live production, with Replay, League Exchange, AutoData and OTT alongside [sp-08, sp-19].
free.who_for: Professional and semi-professional clubs, academies, universities and leagues that want permanent multi-pitch capture with no server on site and a shared video and data workflow, with the A-Line announced for pre-order in March 2026 as the cheaper route for smaller venues [sp-09, sp-03, sp-14]. Grassroots teams with one pitch and one camera budget are served better by the portable vendors, since Spiideo publishes no list price and sells by quote [sp-19, sp-08].
free.why: The Roma case shows the pattern Spiideo is built for: a club with several pitches that wants the whole training ground recorded every day, where a PoE camera feeding a cloud platform removes both the operator and the on-site server [sp-14, sp-07, sp-09]. It matters now because revenue reached 243 million Swedish kronor in 2025 with losses still at 56 million, a 20 million dollar round in 2024 and the Signality tracking acquisition point to a company buying its way into data, and AI Highlights in May 2026 shows production automation moving from camera control to editorial [sp-06, sp-01, sp-02, sp-04]. My reading is that the space is splitting, with one camp selling cheap capture to amateurs and Spiideo betting that leagues, federations and academies will pay for capture, data and broadcast in one cloud, which is the audience its 2026 launches name [sp-04].
free.price_band: Quote-only; the one published partner price is USD 1,875 per team package for 25 games with AutoData stats and 50 hours of storage in a US hockey programme, and Spiideo claims the A-Line is up to 44 percent cheaper than comparable systems

italy.note: AS Roma automates capture on four training pitches with Spiideo Perform, the Milan youth academy SSD Ausonia 1931 installed cameras on three pitches on Inter's recommendation, Inter Milan is named as a customer by Sportico, and Spiideo lists Italy as a remote office location and offers Italian on its support site [sp-14, sp-15, sp-22, sp-16, sp-23].

free.evidence_note: Company financials come from the Swedish register via allabolag and product facts from Spiideo pages and help articles, but there is no public price list, the only price is a US partner package, security and data location documents are absent from the public site, and reviewer volume is tiny.

free.name: Veo Technologies
free.payer_model_label: Club pays for a coaching tool
free.one_line: Veo sells a tripod-mounted twin-lens camera (Veo Cam 3) and a two-iPhone variant (Veo Go) that record the whole pitch unattended, then stitch, follow the ball and cut highlights in the cloud for a subscription fee [veo-06, veo-22].
free.who_for: Amateur and youth football clubs, schools and academies that want match and training video without a camera operator, with the club or team owning the camera and paying a yearly plan per camera [veo-04, veo-02]. Veo Go extends the same platform to teams that already own two recent iPhones and want to spend under 300 euros a year [veo-02, veo-22].
free.why: Veo exists because grassroots clubs wanted the analysis habit of professional football without the staff, and a 1,299 euro camera plus a 579 to 1,159 euro yearly plan made that habit affordable [veo-02]. It matters now because the company has crossed 500 million Danish kroner in revenue and cut its annual loss to under 5 million kroner in 2025, which puts it closer to breakeven than any other portable camera vendor whose accounts I have read [veo-08]. The Lega Nazionale Dilettanti partnership of September 2025 and the free Analytics 2 bundle running to 30 September 2026 show where the space is going, with hardware treated as a loss leader and the money made on data and analytics add-ons [veo-11, veo-05].
free.price_band: €1,299 camera (€1,599 for the 5G model) plus €579 to €1,979 per year for Editor plans, with Analytics 2, Live and Player Spotlight add-ons priced separately; Veo Go from €279 per year with the phone rig and tripod included on yearly terms

italy.note: Veo is an official partner of the Lega Nazionale Dilettanti since 8 September 2025, sells in Italian through veo.com/it with Cittadella, Südtirol, Como and AC Crema shown as customers, and is resold by the analysis software house Sics as an official partner [veo-11, veo-13, veo-26].

free.name: zone14
free.payer_model_label: Club pays for a coaching tool
free.one_line: zone14 rents Austrian built fixed 4K twin camera systems to football clubs on a subscription from EUR 115 to about EUR 130 a month, bundled with its REPLAY analysis software and optional video based player fitness data [zone14-01, zone14-02, zone14-03].
free.who_for: Amateur, semi professional and academy football clubs in German speaking Europe and Croatia that want every home match and training session recorded from a permanent mount and analysed by their own coaches [zone14-02, zone14-04]. It suits clubs that own or control their ground, since the cameras are mains powered and installed once [zone14-02].
free.why: zone14 exists because two Viennese founders saw that amateur clubs training four times a week wanted professional style video analysis and that no fixed camera came bundled with the software and the data to do it, so they built the camera, the analysis tool and a video based tracking layer as one subscription [zone14-05, zone14-02]. It matters now because the Bavarian football association made it official technology partner for more than 4,500 clubs and SK Rapid and Austria Wien's academy use it, which shows a European coaching first alternative to the broadcast and parent led models can reach scale [zone14-06, zone14-07]. It tells you that in Europe the buyer with the steadiest budget is still the club, and that a vendor that replaces GPS vests with video data has a second reason to be paid.

free.name: BallerCam (Baller, Inc. / BallerTV)
free.payer_model_label: Family or coach buys the device
free.one_line: BallerCam is a $299 shell with a 180-degree lens, cooling fan and battery that turns an iPhone 13 Pro or newer into an AI camera that records, livestreams and clips youth basketball, soccer, futsal and volleyball games [ballercam-01, ballercam-02].
free.who_for: US and Canadian parents, team managers and club coaches who already own a recent iPhone and want automated filming and free livestreaming without a per-viewer or per-team subscription [ballercam-01, ballercam-08]. It is a family product first, and coaches use it because the footage and clips come free of per-seat fees [ballercam-06].
free.why: BallerTV built BallerCam because eight years of streaming more than two million youth games with paid crews and fixed cameras taught it that the unit economics only work if the family owns the capture device, so it packaged its computer vision into a phone shell and launched it in July 2025 with Alex Morgan as investor and face [ballercam-03, ballercam-04]. It matters now because a $299 one-off device with a free 20-hour cloud tier undercuts every fixed camera with a mandatory subscription and pushes the category toward hardware-light, app-heavy products [ballercam-02, ballercam-05]. It tells you the youth capture market is splitting into two, a club tier that buys a dedicated camera and a family tier that buys an accessory for the phone it already carries, and that the second tier will be won on app reliability and storage economics [ballercam-06, ballercam-07].
free.price_band: $299 one-off device (list $349); cloud storage free for 20 hours, $99/yr for 100 hours, $199/yr for 250 hours

italy.note: New devices ship only to the US and Canada, the app works anywhere with an iPhone and connectivity, and the terms state the service is intended for users in the United States [ballercam-08, ballercam-11].

free.name: FoloCam (FoloCam LLC)
free.payer_model_label: Family or coach buys the device
free.one_line: FoloCam is an iOS app that pairs an iPhone 13 or newer with an Apple DockKit motorised gimbal and uses on-device AI to keep the ball in frame for soccer and basketball, recording 4K locally for $49.99 a year [folocam-01, folocam-02].
free.who_for: Parents and volunteer coaches who already own a recent iPhone and want a full-match recording that follows the ball for the price of a cheap gimbal and a low subscription, with no cloud account and no hardware lock-in [folocam-01, folocam-03]. It suits people who are comfortable with a one-developer product and will handle their own storage and sharing [folocam-03].
free.why: FoloCam exists because Apple's DockKit framework and the Neural Engine in recent iPhones made it possible for a single developer, Gilbert Chen of Duplicacy and ActionStitch, to ship a ball-tracking camera as a $49.99 app, where the incumbents ship a $1,000 device [folocam-03, folocam-05]. It matters now because it sets the floor price for automated football filming at roughly $100 of gimbal plus $50 a year, with all processing on the phone and no video leaving the device, which is a privacy posture the cloud-based incumbents cannot match [folocam-02, folocam-04]. It tells you the capture layer is commoditising fast, that the value is moving to the platform and analysis layers, and that solo and small developers can now attack the low end of the market from the App Store [folocam-05, folocam-06].
free.price_band: App free for 10-minute recordings; $49.99/yr (€59.99/yr in Italy) for unlimited recording and RTMP; $150 Amazon kit with gimbal and lifetime subscription; DockKit gimbal from about $35 to $100 extra

italy.note: The app is listed on the Italian App Store with the Premium Yearly in-app purchase at €59.99, and the gimbals it supports are sold through ordinary consumer retail [folocam-07].

free.evidence_note: Pricing, compatibility, on-device processing and privacy claims verified from FoloCam's site, support page, App Store listings in the US and Italy and the developer's forums; company scale and sentiment from the developer's own statements and a small user forum, with no third-party review found.

free.name: SeeUsPlay (SeeUsPlay, Inc.)
free.payer_model_label: Family or coach buys the device
free.one_line: SeeUsPlay is a dual-GoPro rig and app whose cloud AI turns two standard action cameras into an automatically tracked full-game video and highlight clips, paid for with tokens per game with no subscription [seeusplay-01, seeusplay-02].
free.who_for: Youth and amateur teams, mostly in the US, that want full-field automated recording delivered to YouTube at roughly $14 to $15 a game in 4K without a hardware lock-in or an annual fee [seeusplay-01, seeusplay-03]. It suits team managers who are happy to own GoPros, handle SD-card uploads and wait a few hours for processing [seeusplay-04].
free.why: SeeUsPlay exists because standard GoPros already produce better raw video than most proprietary youth cameras, so the founders moved all the intelligence to the cloud and sold only a mount, a token and a processing job [seeusplay-01, seeusplay-05]. It matters now because token pricing with no off-season cost, full-game downloads on every plan and YouTube delivery attack the subscription model that funds Veo, Pixellot and Trace, and because the June 2026 move to 8K with the GoPro MISSION 1 shows a small vendor can ride the action-camera roadmap without building hardware [seeusplay-02, seeusplay-06]. It tells you that once capture is commodity hardware, the difference between vendors is the quality and price of the cloud production job and the terms attached to the footage [seeusplay-03, seeusplay-07].
free.price_band: Rig bundles $199 to $499 (sale prices, list $249 to $599) plus own GoPros; tokens $349 per 100 or $599 per 200 on sale, with a 4K game costing 4 tokens, 5K 5 tokens and 8K 10 tokens

free.name: XbotGo (Blink Tech, Inc.)
free.hq: Mountain View, California, United States (with offices in Texas, Beijing, Shenzhen and Suzhou)

free.one_line: XbotGo sells two consumer AI tracking cameras, the Chameleon phone gimbal from about USD 300 and the standalone 4K Falcon from USD 799, with tracking, livestream and 20 GB cloud storage included and paid AI match analysis on top [xbotgo-01, xbotgo-02, xbotgo-12].

It tells you that the venue-network subscription model, where the platform owns cameras and viewers and the club owns nothing, is what private equity is paying for, and that Europe has no equivalent at this scale [livebarn-01, livebarn-02].

free.one_line: Joymo is a Norwegian OTT platform for grassroots and federation sport that lets clubs stream from a phone, encoder or camera and sell access to viewers with safeguarding controls built in [joymo-01, joymo-02].
free.who_for: County FAs, schools, universities and governing bodies in the UK and Norway that want a branded, paywalled channel with consent tooling for filming minors [joymo-02, joymo-03]. It suits organisations that prioritise safeguarding and control over maximum reach [joymo-02].
free.why: Joymo exists because grassroots bodies wanted the revenue of streaming without the exposure of public platforms, so it built a controlled-access OTT product with GDPR training, consent templates and overview framing as part of the offer [joymo-02]. It matters now because Spiideo, an automated camera vendor, is its largest shareholder at 18.8 percent and its partner for a UK education bundle since July 2025, which shows camera companies buying their way into the distribution layer [joymo-04, joymo-05]. It tells you the distribution platforms next to this category are small, loss-making and being absorbed into camera vendors' ecosystems, with Joymo posting a NOK 17 million pre-tax loss on NOK 9.7 million revenue in 2025 [joymo-06].
free.price_band: Free for the club to join in county FA deals; minimum pay-per-view ticket £3.99; club keeps 55 percent of gross profit after payment fees, VAT and streaming costs

italy.note: Joymo's public partnerships are in the UK, Norway and international federations such as World Boxing, and no Italian partner or Italian-language offer was found [joymo-01, joymo-07].

free.evidence_note: Minimum PPV price and 55/45 split come from the Lancashire FA FAQ hosted by The FA, which dates from the 2021 partnership and may have been revised; company financials and shareholders from the Norwegian register via Proff; Joymo's own FAQ pages do not publish current prices.

free.name: Min Fotboll (Svenska Fotbollförbundet)
free.payer_model_label: Distribution layer, club and viewer split
free.one_line: Min Fotboll is the Swedish FA's official app, in which volunteers stream matches from a phone or a connected Veo or Spiideo camera and viewers pay SEK 59 for 30 days of every youth match in Sweden, with half the revenue after VAT going to a club of the viewer's choice [minfotboll-01, minfotboll-02].
free.who_for: Every Swedish club, from children's teams to lower senior divisions, since the app is free to use, tied to the FA's competition database and the only place SvFF sanctions youth streaming [minfotboll-01, minfotboll-03]. Families and grandparents who want to follow a child's team anywhere in the country are the paying audience [minfotboll-01].
free.why: Min Fotboll exists because the Swedish FA decided that grassroots streaming, sponsorship and communication should sit inside one federation-owned app, away from fragmented commercial platforms, and it framed GDPR control as a reason from the start [minfotboll-03, minfotboll-04]. It matters now because it is the clearest example of a federation owning the distribution and checkout layer and treating camera vendors such as Veo and Spiideo as interchangeable inputs, with nearly 11,500 livestreams and 126,000 matches with user content in 2024 [minfotboll-01, minfotboll-05]. It tells you that where a federation moves first, the automated camera becomes a peripheral and the pricing power moves to the app that holds the fixtures [minfotboll-02, minfotboll-06].
free.price_band: Free for clubs; youth viewer pass SEK 59 per 30 days for all youth matches; senior PPV set by the club; club replay package SEK 2,000 per year; 50 percent of revenue after VAT to the chosen club

italy.note: Min Fotboll is a Swedish federation service available only for Swedish competitions and has no presence outside Sweden [minfotboll-01, minfotboll-03].

free.evidence_note: Viewer price, revenue share, replay package and camera integrations verified from the Swedish FA's own livestreaming page; usage numbers from SvFF articles; Veo partnership from the SvFF press release; launch year inferred from SvFF's 2023 article and flagged in unverified.

free.name: Solidsport
free.payer_model_label: Distribution layer, club and viewer split
free.one_line: Solidsport is a Swedish streaming platform that lets clubs, leagues and federations broadcast matches from any camera, including Veo, and sell them to viewers on a 50/50 revenue split after VAT [solidsport-01, solidsport-02].
free.who_for: Clubs and federations in the Nordics, Germany and Austria that want a free-to-join channel with pay-per-view, season passes and supporter subscriptions and are willing to trade half the gross for a turnkey platform [solidsport-01, solidsport-03]. It suits organisations that already own an automated camera and want a place to monetise the feed [solidsport-04].
free.why: Solidsport exists because grassroots clubs had cameras and audiences but no way to charge for a stream, so it built a channel platform that costs the club nothing upfront and splits the gross [solidsport-01, solidsport-02]. It matters now because federation-wide deals such as SHFV in June 2025 and the Swedish Handball extension in September 2025 turn it into the default distribution layer that camera vendors plug into, and revenue grew 42 percent to SEK 85 million in 2025 on that model [solidsport-03, solidsport-05, solidsport-06]. It tells you that in Europe the money in automated match video is being made by whoever owns the checkout page, and that camera vendors without a monetisation layer end up as suppliers to platforms like this one [solidsport-04, solidsport-07].
free.price_band: Free for the club to join; viewers pay club-set PPV or subscription prices above a Solidsport minimum; gross split 50/50 after VAT

italy.note: The site lists Sweden, Finland, Germany, Slovenia, Austria and Serbia as markets and no Italian federation, league or club partner was found [solidsport-01].

free.evidence_note: Revenue split, price setting and payout terms verified from Solidsport's own terms, the Veo integration from Solidsport's guide, the SHFV deal from Solidsport's press release, and 2025 revenue from the Swedish company register via Allabolag.

free.name: Staylive (StayLive AB, part of Two Circles)
free.payer_model_label: Distribution layer, club and viewer split
free.one_line: Staylive is a Swedish white-label OTT platform, owned by Two Circles since its 2024 purchase of Spring Media Group, that gives leagues, federations and youth operators such as Minnesota's Youth Sports Plus a branded streaming service with payments and apps [staylive-01, staylive-02, staylive-03].
free.who_for: Leagues, federations and aggregators that want their own branded streaming destination on iOS, Android and Apple TV with integrated payments under their own brand [staylive-01]. In youth sport it serves operators like Youth Sports Plus, which feeds Spiideo camera output into MNHockey.tv across 25,000 games a season [staylive-02, staylive-04].
free.why: Staylive exists because Nordic leagues in hockey, bandy and basketball wanted to own their streaming product outright, with no rented channel, and Spring Media built it as the technology arm of a rights and production group [staylive-01, staylive-05]. It matters now because Two Circles bought the group in October 2024 and is pushing Staylive as a global platform provider, which puts a large agency behind a product that automated cameras feed into at youth level [staylive-03, staylive-06]. It tells you that distribution for automated match video is consolidating into agency-owned platforms, and that the camera vendor rarely owns the viewer relationship in these deals [staylive-02, staylive-04].
free.price_band: White-label platform fees not published; viewer prices set by the rights holder; MNHockey.tv app reviews cite roughly $9 charges without an official price list

italy.note: Named customers are Nordic leagues, INDYCAR Live, Eredivisie and European swimming bodies, with no Italian rights holder found [staylive-01].

free.evidence_note: Ownership and the Youth Sports Plus deal are verified from Staylive's and SportsPro's pages, but no viewer prices, platform fees or revenue shares are published, and the Staylive news feed has no entries after October 2024.
